Optical storageAppend-only, yet any data structure

    

      
log = []                # a write-once disc

      
def node(key, left=None, right=None):

      
    log.append((key, left, right)) # the only write

      
    return len(log) - 1     # pointer = position

      
def insert(root, key):   # returns a NEW root

      
    if root is None: return node(key)

      
    k, l, r = log[root]

      
    if key < k: return node(k, insert(l, key), r)

      
    return node(k, l, insert(r, key))

      
v1 = None

      
for k in (5, 3, 8): v1 = insert(v1, k)

      
v2 = insert(v1, 4)

    

    
python ptree.py

    
THE DISC: NODES IN WRITE ORDER

Block devicesThe OS sees an array of blocks

    

      
#define BSIZE 512          // one sector

      
struct block { unsigned char b[BSIZE]; };

      
void bread(int id, struct block *buf);

      
void bwrite(int id, const struct block *buf);

      
 

      
void write_byte(long off, unsigned char c) {

      
    struct block buf;

      
    bread(off / BSIZE, &buf);  // 1. read the whole block

      
    buf.b[off % BSIZE] = c;      // 2. change one byte

      
    bwrite(off / BSIZE, &buf); // 3. write it all back

      
}

    

    
./bdev

    
THE DISK: BLOCKS 0 TO 63

    

    
MEMORY: struct block buf (512 BYTES)

    

    
    

    
The device moves whole blocks only: one changed byte costs 1,024 moved

FAT320 sectors: where does each file live?

    
The first IBM PC floppy: 40 tracks × 8 sectors × 512 bytes = 160 KiB

    

    
    
Idea 1: each sector ends with "next"to reach sector 4 of a file, read sectors 1 to 3 first

    
Idea 2: all "next" pointers in one table at the frontread the table once, keep it in memory, jump anywhere

    

    
Pull the next pointers into one table: the File Allocation Table

    
160 KiB single-sided 5.25-inch PC floppy (1981); FAT came from Microsoft's disk BASIC and MS-DOS · the file's sector numbers here are an example, not from a real disk

  

  

    

    
FATfat32.img: the boot sector, field by field

    
bytes 0x00-0x5f and 0x1f0-0x1ff of fat32.img

    

      
BytsPerSec, = unpack_from('<H', img, 0x0B)  # 512

      
SecPerClus  = img[0x0D]                     # 1

      
RsvdSecCnt, = unpack_from('<H', img, 0x0E)  # 32

      
NumFATs     = img[0x10]                     # 2

      
TotSec32,   = unpack_from('<I', img, 0x20)  # 131072 = 64 MiB

      
FATSz32,    = unpack_from('<I', img, 0x24)  # 1009

      
RootClus,   = unpack_from('<I', img, 0x2C)  # 2

      
Signature   = img[0x1FE:0x200]              # b'\x55\xaa'

    

    

    

    
Eight numbers from one sector tell us where everything else is

    
Bytes: fatbytes.py on the course's fat32.img (source/code/fatbytes.out); code lines: readfat.py, after the source lecture's readfat.c; field offsets: Microsoft FAT32 File System Specification (2000), section 3

  

  

    

    
FATWhere does cluster 2 start?

    

    

      
def cluster_to_off(n):        # data clusters are numbered from 2

      
    DataSec = RsvdSecCnt + NumFATs * FATSz32

      
    return (DataSec + (n - 2) * SecPerClus) * BytsPerSec

    

    

    
python fatbytes.py fat32.img

    
Two multiplications turn a cluster number into a byte offset

    
Numbers from fatbytes.py on fat32.img (source/code/fatbytes.out) · code: readfat.py · bar not to scale (the data area is 98% of the disk)

  

  

    

    
FATA directory is a file of 32-byte entries

An entry holds the name, the size, and the first cluster, nothing more

FATFollow the chain in the FAT

    

    
    

      
def next_cluster(n):        # 4 bytes per entry

      
    off = RsvdSecCnt * BytsPerSec

      
    return unpack_from('<I', img, off + 4*n)[0] & 0x0FFFFFFF

      
c = first

      
while 2 <= c < CLUS_INVALID:  # 0x0FFFFFF8 and up: end

      
    chain.append(c); c = next_cluster(c)

    

    
python fatbytes.py fat32.img

    
A file is a linked list in the FAT: sequential is easy, a jump walks the list

    
FAT entries and chains: fatbytes.py on fat32.img (source/code/fatbytes.out) · code: readfat.py, after the source lecture's readfat.c

  

  

    

    
inodeUNIX: names in directories, files in inodes

    

    
    

    
FAT: metadata in the directory entry, so no hard linksext2: an entry is just name + inode number, so many names can share one inode

    
Split the name from the file: the inode holds everything but the name
